title: Antibiotics and Alcohol: Which Ones Clash and How Long to Wait
excerpt: Can you drink on antibiotics? Which antibiotics really clash with alcohol (metronidazole, tinidazole, linezolid), which are low risk, how long to wait, and warning signs.
metaDescription: Can you drink on antibiotics? Which ones clash with alcohol, like metronidazole, which are low risk, how long to wait, and the warning signs to know.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** most common antibiotics, including amoxicillin, azithromycin, cephalexin, doxycycline, and ciprofloxacin, have no dangerous direct interaction with a moderate amount of alcohol. A drink or two is unlikely to stop them working or cause a chemical reaction. But a handful of antibiotics really do clash with alcohol, sometimes badly, and the main ones are **metronidazole (Flagyl)** and **tinidazole (Tindamax)**, which many people are told to avoid alcohol with during the course and for three days after. A few others, such as **linezolid**, some hospital cephalosporins, and the tuberculosis drugs, carry their own specific warnings. And even when there's no interaction, drinking while you're fighting an infection tends to make you feel worse and recover slower.

**The quick rules:** Check the name of your antibiotic against the table below. If it's metronidazole, tinidazole, or secnidazole, don't drink at all during the course or for at least three days after the last dose (check your label for the exact window), and watch for hidden alcohol in mouthwash and liquid medicines. If it's linezolid, avoid tap beer and other high-tyramine drinks. For most other antibiotics, an occasional light drink is generally considered low risk, but skipping alcohol until you finish the course and feel better is the safer and kinder choice for your body.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and label guidance. It is not a substitute for the doctor or pharmacist who prescribed your antibiotic and knows your health history. **Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before drinking if** you're unsure which antibiotic you're on, you take more than one medicine, you have liver disease, or your infection is serious. **Get medical help right away if** you have trouble breathing, swelling of the face, lips, or throat, a widespread rash, chest pain, fainting, or severe vomiting after drinking on any medication. In an emergency, call 911.

## Why Some Antibiotics Clash With Alcohol: The Mechanism in Plain Words

"Antibiotics" isn't one drug. It's a large group of very different medicines that happen to share a job: killing bacteria or stopping them from multiplying. They're built from different chemical families, broken down by different routes in the body, and they have different side effects. That's why a single rule like "never drink on antibiotics" is both too strict for some drugs and not strict enough for others.

When an antibiotic does clash with alcohol, it's usually through one of four routes.

### 1. Blocking the alcohol clean-up step (the "disulfiram-like" reaction)

When you drink, your liver turns alcohol into a toxic compound called **acetaldehyde**. A second enzyme, called **aldehyde dehydrogenase**, then breaks acetaldehyde down into harmless acetate. Acetaldehyde is a big part of why heavy drinking makes you feel sick.

A drug called **disulfiram (Antabuse)** works by blocking that second enzyme on purpose, so acetaldehyde piles up and drinking makes you feel awful. Some antibiotics have been linked to a similar reaction, which doctors call "disulfiram-like." The symptoms are:

- Flushing and warmth in the face and neck
- A throbbing headache
- Nausea and vomiting
- A fast or pounding heartbeat
- Shortness of breath
- Dizziness or a drop in blood pressure

This is the reaction behind the strongest antibiotic-and-alcohol warnings, and it's mostly tied to metronidazole, tinidazole, and a few cephalosporins.

### 2. Adding to the same side effects

Many antibiotics can cause nausea, an upset stomach, diarrhea, dizziness, or tiredness. Alcohol causes all of those too. Even without any chemical interaction, stacking the two can make you feel noticeably worse. With some drugs, such as the fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin), dizziness or feeling foggy is a known side effect, and alcohol can add to it.

### 3. Changing how the drug is processed

Regular heavy drinking changes how the liver handles some medicines. With **doxycycline**, for example, the label notes that chronic heavy alcohol use can lower drug levels in the blood, possibly making it less effective. This is about a pattern of heavy drinking, not one beer.

### 4. Extra strain on the liver

A few antibiotics, most notably the tuberculosis drug **isoniazid**, can injure the liver on their own. Daily alcohol use raises that risk. Here the issue isn't a reaction at the table. It's two things that each stress the liver, added together over weeks or months.

## Antibiotics and Alcohol: Drug-by-Drug Table

Here's where the common antibiotics stand. This is general label guidance, not a substitute for your own prescription label or pharmacist.

| Antibiotic (common brand) | Alcohol interaction | General guidance |
|---|---|---|
| Metronidazole (Flagyl) | Disulfiram-like reaction warning | Avoid during the course and for at least 3 days after |
| Tinidazole (Tindamax) | Disulfiram-like reaction warning | Avoid during the course and for 3 days after |
| Secnidazole (Solosec) | Same drug family as metronidazole | Ask your pharmacist; many avoid alcohol around the dose |
| Cefotetan, cefoperazone (mostly hospital IV drugs) | Disulfiram-like reaction reported | Avoid during treatment and for about 3 days after |
| Linezolid (Zyvox) | Reacts with tyramine | Avoid tap beer, some craft and unpasteurized beers, and some red wines |
| Sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim (Bactrim, Septra) | Occasional reaction reports; shared side effects | Many prescribers advise avoiding or limiting alcohol |
| Isoniazid, rifampin (tuberculosis) | Higher liver injury risk with daily drinking | Avoid alcohol; follow your clinic's advice |
| Doxycycline (Vibramycin, Doryx) | Heavy drinking may lower drug levels | Moderate drinking generally fine; avoid heavy drinking |
| Amoxicillin, penicillin | No significant direct interaction | Light drinking generally considered low risk |
| Amoxicillin-clavulanate (Augmentin) | No significant direct interaction | Alcohol may worsen stomach upset and diarrhea |
| Azithromycin (Zithromax, Z-Pak) | No significant direct interaction | Light drinking generally considered low risk |
| Cephalexin (Keflex), cefdinir, cefuroxime | No significant direct interaction | Light drinking generally considered low risk |
| Ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin | No direct reaction; dizziness can stack | Go easy; avoid if you feel dizzy or foggy |
| Nitrofurantoin (Macrobid) | No significant direct interaction | Alcohol may add to nausea and dizziness |
| Clindamycin (Cleocin) | No significant direct interaction | Alcohol can worsen stomach upset and diarrhea |

"Generally considered low risk" means low risk for a healthy adult having a drink or two. It doesn't mean drinking is a good idea while you're sick, and it doesn't apply to binge drinking.

## Metronidazole and Alcohol: The One Everyone Asks About

Metronidazole (brand name Flagyl) is the antibiotic most associated with "absolutely no alcohol." It's prescribed for bacterial vaginosis, trichomoniasis, some dental and gum infections, some stomach and gut infections, and certain infections after surgery.

The label warns that drinking alcohol while taking it, or within three days of stopping it, can cause abdominal cramps, nausea, vomiting, headaches, and flushing. That's the disulfiram-like reaction described above.

### Is the metronidazole reaction real?

This is an area where researchers have argued. A review published in *Annals of Pharmacotherapy* in 2000 looked at the evidence and concluded that the case for a true disulfiram-like reaction was weaker than most people assume, and that many reported cases had other possible explanations. Some small studies have also failed to show the reaction reliably.

That doesn't mean it's safe to drink. Case reports of serious reactions exist, the official label still carries the warning, and you can't predict whether you'll be one of the people who reacts. The sensible reading of the debate is that the reaction may be less common than legend says, but it's not worth testing on yourself. The practical advice hasn't changed: **no alcohol during metronidazole or for at least three days afterward.**

### Watch for hidden alcohol

If you're on metronidazole or tinidazole, alcohol can sneak in from places you wouldn't think of:

- **Mouthwash.** Many popular mouthwashes contain alcohol. Choose an alcohol-free one.
- **Liquid medicines.** Some cough syrups and liquid cold remedies contain alcohol. Check the label or ask the pharmacist.
- **Kombucha.** It naturally contains a small amount of alcohol.
- **Cooking.** Dishes with wine or spirits added near the end of cooking can still hold some alcohol.
- **"Non-alcoholic" beer and wine.** Many still contain a trace (often labeled as under 0.5%). Most people would be fine, but if you've reacted before, skip it.

## Tinidazole, Secnidazole, and Other Drugs in the Same Family

**Tinidazole** (Tindamax) is a close relative of metronidazole, used for many of the same infections. Its label carries the same kind of alcohol warning: avoid alcohol during treatment and for three days after.

**Secnidazole** (Solosec) is a newer single-dose drug in the same family, used for bacterial vaginosis and trichomoniasis. Because it's in the same chemical group, ask your pharmacist how long to avoid alcohol around your dose.

## Cephalosporins: Mostly Fine, With a Few Exceptions

Cephalosporins are a big antibiotic family. The ones you're most likely to get from a regular doctor or urgent care, such as **cephalexin (Keflex)**, cefdinir, cefuroxime, and cefadroxil, don't have a known significant interaction with alcohol.

A few cephalosporins do. Drugs such as **cefotetan** and **cefoperazone** have a particular chemical side group that can block the alcohol clean-up enzyme, causing a disulfiram-like reaction. These are mostly given by IV in hospitals, so most people won't run into them at home. If you were treated in hospital and are unsure what you got, ask before your first drink after discharge.

## Linezolid: The Tap Beer Problem

Linezolid (Zyvox) is a stronger antibiotic used for serious infections, including some resistant ones like MRSA. Its alcohol issue is different. Linezolid weakly blocks an enzyme called monoamine oxidase, which also breaks down **tyramine**, a substance found in aged, fermented, and cured foods.

If tyramine builds up, it can cause a sudden, dangerous rise in blood pressure. Some alcoholic drinks are high in tyramine, especially **tap or draft beer, unpasteurized and some craft beers, and certain red wines**. The linezolid label advises avoiding large amounts of tyramine-rich foods and drinks. If you're on linezolid, ask your pharmacist for a list of what to avoid, and get help right away for a severe headache, chest pain, or a pounding heartbeat.

## Bactrim (Sulfamethoxazole-Trimethoprim)

Bactrim is common for urinary tract infections, some skin infections, and other uses. There are scattered case reports of disulfiram-like reactions when it's combined with alcohol, though the link is less established than with metronidazole. Bactrim can also cause nausea and, rarely, liver problems, and long-term heavy drinking adds to both. Many doctors and pharmacists advise skipping or keeping alcohol to a minimum during a Bactrim course. That's a reasonable default.

## Tuberculosis Antibiotics: A Longer-Term Liver Issue

Tuberculosis treatment usually lasts months, not days, and drugs such as **isoniazid** and **rifampin** can strain the liver. Daily alcohol use raises the chance of liver injury from isoniazid. TB clinics usually advise avoiding alcohol during treatment and monitor liver function with blood tests. If you're being treated for TB or latent TB, follow your clinic's advice on alcohol closely, and report nausea, loss of appetite, dark urine, or yellow skin or eyes promptly.

## Does Alcohol Make Antibiotics Less Effective?

This is the other big worry: "Will a drink cancel out my antibiotics?" For most antibiotics, the answer is **no**. A moderate amount of alcohol doesn't stop amoxicillin, azithromycin, cephalexin, or most other common antibiotics from killing bacteria.

There are a few ways drinking can still get in the way, though:

- **Heavy drinking and doxycycline.** As mentioned above, chronic heavy drinking can lower doxycycline levels.
- **Missed or vomited doses.** A late night can mean a skipped dose, a dose taken hours late, or throwing up a pill you just swallowed. Antibiotics work best when blood levels stay steady, so this matters more than people think.
- **Your immune system does part of the work.** Antibiotics knock bacteria back, but your immune system finishes the job. Heavy drinking can temporarily weaken immune responses, disrupt sleep, and dehydrate you. Our guide to [alcohol and the immune system](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-immune-system-complete-health-impact-2025) explains how.

So the honest version is: alcohol rarely "cancels" an antibiotic directly, but drinking heavily while sick can make your recovery slower and messier.

## Can You Drink on Antibiotics? Where the "Never" Rule Came From

Plenty of people grew up hearing that you must never touch alcohol on any antibiotic. For most antibiotics, that blanket rule isn't supported by drug-interaction evidence. So where did it come from?

Nobody knows for certain. One story often repeated by doctors is that clinics treating sexually transmitted infections with penicillin in the mid-20th century told patients to avoid alcohol, partly in the hope that staying sober would also mean avoiding new sexual partners during treatment. That story is plausible but hard to verify, so treat it as folklore. What's more likely is that the warning spread because a few antibiotics genuinely do react with alcohol, and a simple "never" rule was easier to give than a list.

The rule isn't useless, though. Avoiding alcohol on antibiotics does three real things: it protects you from the drugs that do clash, it avoids stacking side effects, and it gives your body a better shot at recovering. If you're sick enough to need antibiotics, a few dry days rarely hurt.

## Strep Throat, Tooth Infections, and UTIs: Common Scenarios

Here's how the general rules apply to the infections people ask about most.

### Strep throat

Strep throat is usually treated with **penicillin or amoxicillin**, or with **cephalexin, azithromycin, or clindamycin** for people allergic to penicillin. None of these has a significant direct interaction with alcohol. That said, alcohol can irritate an already raw throat and add to dehydration, and strep can make you feel run-down. Most people feel better within a day or two of starting treatment. Waiting until then, and finishing the full course, is the better plan.

### Tooth infections

Dental infections are commonly treated with **amoxicillin, amoxicillin-clavulanate (Augmentin), penicillin, or clindamycin**. These don't have a significant direct interaction with alcohol. The catch is that dentists sometimes add or switch to **metronidazole** for certain gum and tooth infections, and that one does carry the strict alcohol warning. If you were given more than one antibiotic for a tooth problem, check each name. Also, if you're taking a prescription painkiller after dental work, alcohol is a bad mix with many of those regardless of the antibiotic.

### Urinary tract infections

UTIs are commonly treated with **nitrofurantoin (Macrobid), Bactrim, fosfomycin, cephalexin**, or sometimes **ciprofloxacin**. Of these, Bactrim is the one most often paired with "avoid alcohol." Beyond drug interactions, alcohol is a diuretic and a bladder irritant for many people, which can make urgency and burning feel worse. Drinking plenty of water helps a UTI; drinking alcohol doesn't.

### Bacterial vaginosis and trichomoniasis

These are usually treated with **metronidazole, tinidazole, or secnidazole**, all from the family with the strongest alcohol warnings. This is the scenario where "no alcohol" really means no alcohol, including the three-day window after you finish.

## How Long After Antibiotics Can You Drink?

It depends entirely on the drug.

- **Metronidazole and tinidazole:** wait at least **3 days (72 hours)** after your last dose. Some older advice said 48 hours, but current labels use three days.
- **Cefotetan and similar hospital cephalosporins:** about **3 days** after the last dose.
- **Linezolid:** the tyramine caution applies during treatment. Ask your pharmacist when it's safe to resume high-tyramine drinks.
- **Isoniazid and other TB drugs:** follow your clinic's advice, which usually covers the whole treatment period.
- **Most other antibiotics** (amoxicillin, azithromycin, cephalexin, doxycycline, and so on): there's no required waiting period from a drug-interaction standpoint. A sensible approach is to finish the course, make sure you're feeling better, and start with a light drink rather than a big night.

One note on azithromycin: it stays in the body for days after a short Z-Pak course. That doesn't create an alcohol reaction, but it's a reminder that "finished the pills" and "drug is gone" aren't the same thing.

## Signs of a Bad Reaction: When to Get Help

Most people who have a drink on a low-risk antibiotic feel nothing unusual. But know the warning signs.

**Signs of a disulfiram-like reaction** (most likely with metronidazole, tinidazole, or certain cephalosporins):

- Sudden flushing of the face and neck
- A throbbing headache
- Nausea and vomiting
- A racing or pounding heart
- Shortness of breath or dizziness

If this happens, stop drinking, sit or lie down, and sip water. Mild reactions usually pass within a few hours. **Get emergency care** if you have chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, severe or nonstop vomiting, or confusion.

**Antibiotic warning signs that have nothing to do with alcohol but get mistaken for a hangover:**

- **Severe, watery, or bloody diarrhea**, especially with stomach cramps or fever, during or after a course. This can be a *C. difficile* infection and needs a doctor. Don't assume it's just from drinking. Our guide to [diarrhea after drinking](/never-hungover/diarrhea-after-drinking) covers the ordinary kind, but antibiotic-linked diarrhea is a different problem.
- **Hives, a spreading rash, or swelling of the face, lips, or tongue.** These can be signs of an allergic reaction. Swelling or trouble breathing is an emergency.
- **Tendon pain or swelling** (often the back of the ankle) while on ciprofloxacin or levofloxacin. Stop exercising and call your doctor.
- **Yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, or pain under the right ribs**, which can signal liver problems.

## Practical Tips If You Do Drink on a Low-Risk Antibiotic

If your doctor or pharmacist has said a drink is fine on your antibiotic, these habits keep the risk low:

1. **Confirm the drug name first.** Check the bottle, not your memory. "The one for my tooth" could be amoxicillin or metronidazole.
2. **Keep it light.** One or two drinks, not a night out.
3. **Don't skip or delay doses.** Set a reminder if you'll be out.
4. **Eat and hydrate.** Many antibiotics are easier on the stomach with food, and alcohol is harder on it without. If your stomach already hurts, our guide to [stomach pain after drinking](/never-hungover/stomach-pain-after-drinking) explains what helps.
5. **Watch your other medicines.** Painkillers, sleep aids, and cold medicines you take alongside an antibiotic can have their own alcohol warnings. Our [medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) covers common ones.
6. **Finish the whole course** even if you feel better, unless your doctor tells you otherwise.

## What About DHM and Other Supplements?

People who use hangover supplements sometimes ask whether they can take them while on antibiotics. The honest answer is that most supplements, DHM included, haven't been well studied alongside antibiotics. There is no good evidence that DHM blocks or reduces a disulfiram-like reaction, and it does nothing to make drinking on metronidazole or tinidazole safer. Don't use any supplement as a workaround for an alcohol warning on your prescription.

If you're on an antibiotic, the simplest approach is to skip new supplements until the course is done, or run them past your pharmacist first. That's also the moment to keep things simple: rest, water, food, and no alcohol.

Once you've finished the course and you're back to normal, DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound some people use around social drinking. Most of the research is from animal and lab studies, with limited human data, so think of it as promising rather than proven. If you want to try it then, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the lower-cost [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers timing and amounts, and our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence, which matter more than any pill.

## The Bottom Line

- Most common antibiotics (amoxicillin, azithromycin, cephalexin, doxycycline, ciprofloxacin, nitrofurantoin) have no dangerous direct interaction with a light amount of alcohol.
- **Metronidazole and tinidazole** are the big exceptions: no alcohol during the course and for at least three days after, including hidden alcohol in mouthwash and liquid medicines.
- **Linezolid** reacts with tyramine in tap beer and some wines; **Bactrim** and **TB drugs** come with their own cautions; a few hospital cephalosporins can cause a disulfiram-like reaction.
- Alcohol rarely "cancels" an antibiotic, but heavy drinking can slow recovery, disrupt doses, and stack side effects.
- When in doubt, ask the pharmacist who filled your prescription. It takes a minute, and they can see your full medication list.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking antibiotics?**

With most common antibiotics, such as amoxicillin, azithromycin, cephalexin, and doxycycline, a light drink is generally considered low risk for a healthy adult. A few antibiotics do clash with alcohol, especially metronidazole and tinidazole, which you should avoid alcohol with during the course and for three days after. Linezolid, Bactrim, some hospital cephalosporins, and tuberculosis drugs also carry cautions. Check your drug name and ask your pharmacist if you're unsure.

**Which antibiotics should you never mix with alcohol?**

The clearest ones are metronidazole (Flagyl) and tinidazole (Tindamax), which can cause a disulfiram-like reaction with flushing, headache, nausea, vomiting, and a racing heart. Some IV cephalosporins such as cefotetan can do the same. Linezolid can react with tyramine in tap beer and some wines, and isoniazid for tuberculosis carries a higher liver risk with daily drinking. Your doctor may advise avoiding alcohol with Bactrim too.

**Does alcohol make antibiotics less effective?**

For most antibiotics, a moderate amount of alcohol doesn't stop them from working. The exceptions are mostly about heavy drinking: chronic heavy drinking can lower doxycycline levels, and a big night can lead to missed, delayed, or vomited doses. Heavy drinking can also weaken your immune response and disrupt sleep, which can slow recovery even when the antibiotic itself still works.

**How long after taking metronidazole can I drink alcohol?**

The label advises avoiding alcohol during treatment and for at least three days (72 hours) after your last dose. Tinidazole has the same three-day guidance. Also avoid hidden sources during that time, such as alcohol-containing mouthwash, some liquid cough and cold medicines, and kombucha.

**Can I drink on amoxicillin?**

Amoxicillin doesn't have a known significant direct interaction with alcohol, so a light drink is generally considered low risk for a healthy adult. Alcohol can still add to side effects like an upset stomach or diarrhea, and it won't help you get over the infection. Waiting until you feel better and finishing the course is the safer choice.

**Can I drink alcohol with antibiotics for a tooth infection?**

It depends on the antibiotic. Amoxicillin, Augmentin, penicillin, and clindamycin don't have a significant direct interaction with alcohol. But dentists sometimes prescribe metronidazole for certain tooth and gum infections, and that one carries a strict no-alcohol warning. Check every antibiotic name you were given, and be careful if you're also taking a prescription painkiller.

**Is it safe to drink on antibiotics for strep throat?**

Strep throat is usually treated with penicillin or amoxicillin, or with cephalexin, azithromycin, or clindamycin for people allergic to penicillin. None of these has a significant direct interaction with alcohol. Alcohol can irritate a sore throat and add to dehydration, though, so most people are better off waiting until they feel better.

**What happens if you accidentally drink on metronidazole?**

Many people feel nothing, but some get a disulfiram-like reaction: flushing, a throbbing headache, nausea, vomiting, and a fast heartbeat. If that happens, stop drinking, rest, and sip water; mild reactions usually pass within hours. Get emergency care for chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, or vomiting you can't stop. Keep taking your antibiotic as prescribed unless a doctor tells you otherwise, and call your pharmacist if you're unsure.
